item.title: Apprenticeship and training in the Canton of Vaud: a practical guide
item.description: How to find an internship in the Canton of Vaud, salary, apprenticeship contract and professional maturity according to Swiss federal law.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Apprenticeship lasts 3-4 years depending on the chosen trade - Combines practical training in the company and theoretical teaching at school - Salary established by the apprenticeship contract, not national - Professional maturity allows continuation of studies after apprenticeship
## Key facts - **What**: Theoretical-practical training program in recognized trades - When: Three or four years according to the chosen professional profile - Where: Training company plus cantonal vocational school - Who: Apprentice, employer, cantonal educational system - Amount: Salary agreed in the apprenticeship contract
### The structure of apprenticeship in Switzerland
In Switzerland, apprenticeship is one of the pillars of the educational system. In the Canton of Vaud, as in the rest of the country, vocational training combines theoretical teaching in vocational school and practical training on the field in a training company. This dual model allows apprentices to acquire concrete skills while continuing their general education.
The duration of the apprenticeship varies according to the chosen trade, typically between three and four years. During this period, the apprentice is subject to federal labor regulations, which include hourly limits and fundamental rights. According to the Swiss regulatory framework, young people under 20 are entitled to a minimum of five weeks of annual leave, while those over 20 benefit from a minimum of four weeks.
The Canton of Vaud, like other Swiss cantons, manages the offer of vocational schools and coordinates with training companies to ensure apprenticeship opportunities in various economic sectors. The responsibility for training is shared between the federal state, which sets professional standards, and the cantons, which organize the administration of school training.
### Salary and apprenticeship contract
The apprentice's salary is not set at the federal level but is agreed upon in the apprenticeship contract between the young person and the employer. In the Canton of Vaud, as in the rest of Switzerland, the apprenticeship contract is the legal document that regulates the rights and duties of both parties.
The contract specifies the duration of the apprenticeship, the monthly or hourly salary, working hours, the apprentice's responsibilities, and the modalities of attendance of theoretical training. Make sure the contract contains all these elements before signing, as it represents the legal basis of the apprenticeship relationship. For more information on salary scenarios and tax deductions, consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator). ### Research and Application Channels in the Canton of Vaud
Finding an apprenticeship position in the Canton of Vaud can be done through various channels. Many companies that train apprentices advertise their opportunities directly on national job portals or through industry federations. The Canton of Vaud, through its professional guidance offices and secondary schools, provides resources and advice to guide young people in their search.
The cantonal chambers of commerce and industry, as well as the Swiss professional associations in various sectors, maintain databases of training companies willing to accept apprentices. It is advisable to start the search at least 12-18 months before the desired start date, as many companies select apprentices in advance. This period allows for evaluating more opportunities and making an informed choice.
### Content of the Apprenticeship Contract
Once a company willing to train has been identified, the apprenticeship contract is signed. This document must contain essential elements: the name of the apprentice and the employer, the trade for which training is provided, the total duration of the apprenticeship (usually 3-4 years), the start date, the remuneration for each year of apprenticeship, weekly working hours, and days off.
The probationary period, typically the first 1-3 months, allows both the apprentice and the employer to assess compatibility. During the probationary period, both parties can terminate the contract with reduced notice periods, often without notice or with a few days' notice. After the probationary period, the termination conditions follow the Swiss federal labor regulations: in the first year, termination is possible with one or two months' notice, from the second to the ninth year with two months, and from the tenth year with three months.
### Organization of School Training
The school component of the apprenticeship takes place at the cantonal vocational school. In the Canton of Vaud, as in other cantons, vocational schools offer theoretical teaching, common subjects (language and mathematics), and specialized disciplines related to the trade. Generally, apprentices attend vocational school one or two days a week, while the remaining days are spent working at the training company.
This dual system allows for continuous learning and progressive acquisition of both theoretical and practical skills. Attendance at the vocational school is mandatory and is part of the apprentice's rights and duties. The costs of attendance are covered by the cantonal public system.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Professional Maturity and Continuing Education
Upon completing the apprenticeship, the apprentice obtains the Federal Vocational Education and Training Certificate (EFZ) in the chosen trade. A significant advantage of the Swiss system is the possibility of obtaining professional maturity during or after the apprenticeship, which opens access to higher education courses at Universities of Applied Sciences (UAS).
Professional maturity includes general subjects (languages, mathematics, sciences) alongside specialized disciplines and requires additional work compared to the standard apprenticeship path. In the Canton of Vaud, as in other Swiss cantons, attendance at professional maturity is funded by the public sector, although the responsibility for organization falls to the cantonal system. Admission requirements and schedules vary slightly between cantons.
### Apprentice Rights According to Federal Law
Apprentices, like all workers in Switzerland, enjoy federal legal protection. Maximum working hours are set at 45 hours per week for sectors such as industry, offices, and retail, while other sectors can reach 50 hours per week. Breaks and rest periods are regulated to protect young workers from the risks of fatigue and dangerous working conditions.
Health insurance (LAMal/KVG) is mandatory for all residents in Switzerland, including apprentices, and must be taken out within three months of starting work. Contributions for federal social insurance (AVS/AHV and AI) begin on the first day of work: the employer pays the social contributions, while the apprentice contributes a share of the wages. These elements are an integral part of the Swiss social protection package.
### Practical Procedure: Checklist to Start an Apprenticeship
Summarizing the concrete steps for those wishing to start an apprenticeship in the Canton of Vaud:
1. Identify trades of interest and consult regional or national databases of training companies. 2. Prepare a complete application with CV, cover letter, and, if possible, school references. 3. Contact training companies directly or respond to apprenticeship offers published online. 4. Once a company is identified, carefully check the apprenticeship contract before signing, ensuring it clearly specifies remuneration, hours, duration, and responsibilities. 5. Register with the cantonal vocational school (the employer will support this step). 6. Take out mandatory health insurance within three months of starting the apprenticeship. 7. Inquire at the Canton of Vaud's career guidance office regarding opportunities for professional maturity if you wish to pursue higher education.
For available apprenticeship offers in the Canton of Vaud and throughout Switzerland, consult the [job offers](nav:jobs) section.

item.title: Vaud Family Allowances: Amounts and How to Apply
item.description: Practical guide to family allowances in the canton of Vaud: how to apply, beneficiaries' rights, required documents and competent compensation fund.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Family allowances: monthly benefit for dependent children, amounts vary by canton - Canton Vaud: specific rights and amounts defined at the cantonal level, can be requested from compensation funds - Procedure: application to be submitted with supporting documents to the competent fund for the economic sector
## Key facts - **What**: Family allowances (Swiss social benefit for families with dependent children) - Where: Each Swiss canton (including Vaud) organizes the system autonomously - Who: Compensation funds for family allowances (cantonal/parity bodies) - Beneficiaries: Parents/guardians of dependent children up to the legal age defined by the canton - Amounts: Vary by canton Vaud and number of children (consult the competent Vaud office for current 2026 data)
Family allowances are a fundamental institution of Swiss social security structured at the cantonal level. Each canton, including Vaud, manages the disbursement of these monthly benefits aimed at parents and guardians of dependent children autonomously. In Vaud, as in all Swiss cantons, family allowances represent an important supplement to family income for those with dependent charges and are an integral part of the social protection system dedicated to families.
The family allowances system in Switzerland operates through specialized compensation funds, public or parity bodies that collect contributions from employers and pay benefits to eligible beneficiaries. Unlike other social benefits managed at the federal level (such as old-age and survivors' insurance AVS/AHV), family allowances remain primarily a cantonal competence. This means that amounts, eligibility conditions, procedures, and age brackets vary from canton to canton, with Vaud having defined its own specific rules and amounts.
### Who is entitled to family allowances
In Vaud, as in the rest of Switzerland, parents or guardians of dependent children who meet specific income, employment, and age conditions are entitled to family allowances. The main categories of beneficiaries include private sector employees, cantonal and municipal public employees, and in certain cases, self-employed workers and farmers.
The maximum age of children for whom allowances are received varies by Swiss canton: generally, allowances are paid until the end of vocational training (apprenticeship) or higher education, or until a certain age threshold (commonly 25 years). In Vaud, a basic monthly amount per child is recognized, with possible supplements for special situations (single-parent family, children in apprenticeship, etc.).
Family allowances do not constitute part of the gross salary and are not subject to deductions for taxes or mandatory insurance. It is a universal social benefit, paid regardless of the amount of salary received (although sometimes subject to income checks for self-employed workers in some cantons). The exact amounts for 2026 in Vaud are not specified in the present source: for current data, it is essential to contact the competent compensation fund for the applicant's work sector or the competent Vaud cantonal office for family welfare. In the canton of Vaud, as in the rest of Switzerland, family allowances are managed by compensation funds (caisse de compensation pour allocations familiales in French). These are specialized entities, generally with a public or paritarian structure (with representations of employers and employees), operating at the cantonal, supra-communal, or sectoral level. Their function is to collect contributions from employers (for each employee) and pay monthly allowances to eligible beneficiaries.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to apply: the first step
The procedure to request family allowances in Vaud begins with identifying the compensation fund competent for your economic sector. The first step is to contact your employer or the relevant trade union: they can provide the name, address, and contacts of the fund designated for your sector. Alternatively, direct recourse to the Vaud cantonal office responsible for social security (Office cantonal de la famille, or equivalent structure of the competent department) allows you to receive complete information and be directed to the correct fund.
### Required documentation
For the submission of the application, the standard documentation usually includes: birth declaration of the children or updated civil status certificate; valid identity document of the applicant; proof of parenthood and cohabitation (e.g., school medical expense receipts, school enrollments, official letters with home addresses); income and employment proofs (recent pay slips, employment letters) — sometimes required by the employer; copy of the Vaud cantonal tax decision of the previous year (in the case of self-employed workers).
### Timeline and deadlines
The application can be submitted at any time of the year, but the allowances are generally backdated to the first day of the month in which the child was born or the applicant started working in the Vaud canton. The processing time normally varies from 2 to 8 weeks from the receipt of the complete application with documentation.
During processing, the fund contacts the employer (if the applicant is an employee) to confirm enrollment, working conditions, and the start date of employment. Family allowances do not require annual renewal but are paid continuously until the condition of right ceases (child reaches the age limit, changes economic sector, moves out of the canton, etc.). However, the fund may request periodic documentary updates (every 2-3 years) to verify the conditions of permanence.
Promptly communicating changes in situation (new child, job change, move, income modification) is essential to avoid recoveries of sums wrongly received. To integrate your calculation of net family income considering family allowances, [consult our salary calculator](nav:calculator). For comparative assessments on the cost of living and other family-related subsidies in Switzerland, visit the [cost of living tool](nav:cost-of-living).

item.title: Apprenticeship and vocational training in the canton of Glarus
item.description: How to find an internship, enter into a contract, learn about the apprentice's salary and achieve professional maturity in the canton of Glarus.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - An EFA apprenticeship lasts 3-4 years depending on the field, alternating between school-based and practical training in a company. - The apprenticeship contract is mandatory by law and regulated by the Code of Obligations. - The salary depends on the canton, the professional field, and the year of apprenticeship; there is no uniform federal minimum wage. - The professional maturity is a complementary certificate that allows access to higher technical schools.
## Key facts - **What**: Dual professional training path with a written contract, lessons in vocational school, and practical training in a company - Where: Canton of Glarus, like all Swiss cantons, offers programs regulated at the federal level - Duration: 3-4 years for EFA, 2 years for practice certificate - Reference law: Federal Law on Vocational and Professional Education and Training and Code of Obligations articles 344-346 - Institutions: Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training, professional associations, SEFRI
Apprenticeship in Switzerland is a proven model that combines theoretical education with direct practical training in a company. In the Canton of Glarus, as in the rest of Switzerland, the path is based on the Federal Law on Vocational and Professional Education and Training and allows young people to acquire nationally recognized professional skills. There are two main options: the EFA (Federal Certificate of Competence), which lasts 3-4 years depending on the chosen field, and the practice certificate, a 2-year path mainly oriented towards company practice.
In both cases, the apprenticeship contract must be concluded in writing between the apprentice (or the person exercising parental responsibility if a minor), the company, and, in some cases, a vocational school or training center. The apprentice's salary varies significantly depending on the reference canton, the professional field, and the year of apprenticeship. There is no uniform federal minimum wage for apprentices in Switzerland, so each canton and field applies its own regulations. In the Canton of Glarus, the amounts are determined by collective agreements and specific cantonal directives.
### How to find an apprenticeship in the Canton of Glarus The search for an apprenticeship position begins with the identification of the professional field of interest. Offers can be found through various channels: cantonal databases, specialized job listing websites, portals of professional associations, and direct contacts with local companies. The Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training of the Canton of Glarus provides free advice and information on companies offering apprenticeships in various sectors.
Once the company has been identified, the candidate must formally apply with a curriculum vitae, cover letter, and school certificates. If the application is successful, a written apprenticeship contract is concluded before the start of the activity. ### The apprenticeship contract and the apprentice's rights
The apprenticeship contract is governed by Articles 344-346 of the Federal Code of Obligations and must contain essential information: names and addresses of the parties, start date and duration, professional branch, working hours, remuneration, amounts for tools and work clothes, and other specific conditions.
Once signed, the contract imposes mutual rights and obligations. The apprentice has the right to receive adequate training, timely remuneration, a safe working environment in accordance with federal workplace safety regulations, and access to vocational school for mandatory lessons. They also have the right to a minimum of 5 weeks of vacation per year if under 20 years old, and 4 weeks for others. The maximum working hours are set at 9 hours per day and 45 hours per week — limits lower than those for adults, reflecting the need to protect young apprentices.
The company, on the other hand, has the right to expect dedication, commitment, and adherence to company rules. Both parties can terminate the contract during the first year without notice; after that, termination follows specific regulations defined by the Federal Vocational and Professional Education and Training Act.
### The apprentice's remuneration: cantonal and branch variability
Remuneration is one of the most requested pieces of information by candidates and their families. Without a uniform federal minimum wage, remuneration is determined by collective agreements between employers' associations and trade unions, and by specific cantonal directives.
In the canton of Glarus, remuneration depends on three factors: the professional branch (some sectors such as finance, healthcare, and construction pay more than retail or gastronomy); the year of apprenticeship (the salary increases progressively from the first to subsequent years); and the collective agreements applicable in the sector (many sectors have signed agreements that set minimum wages for apprentices of each year). To know the amounts in the canton of Glarus and in the branch of interest, it is advisable to contact the Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training, the relevant industry associations, or consult the applicable collective agreements. Training must be in accordance with the Federal Act on Occupational Safety and must protect the apprentice from dangerous or excessively burdensome tasks. Safety regulations are monitored by the competent cantonal authority.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Professional Maturity: The Step Towards Higher Levels
After obtaining the Federal Vocational Education and Training (VET) Certificate, many apprentices choose to continue with the professional maturity, a complementary certificate that recognizes a higher level of general and technical education. Professional maturity allows access to universities of applied sciences (UAS) and some university programs. It can be pursued simultaneously with the apprenticeship (integrated variant) or subsequently (separate variant). In the canton of Glarus, the modalities and providers of professional maturity are indicated by the cantonal office for vocational education and training.
### Step-by-Step Procedure to Apply for an Internship
**Step 1** — Identify the sector: choose the professional sector of interest (mechanics, pharmacy, commerce, IT, electronics, etc.). Step 2 — Research companies: consult job portals and professional association websites to find companies offering internships in your sector. Step 3 — Prepare the application: write a resume, cover letter, and gather school certificates. Step 4 — Apply: send your application to the chosen companies and participate in interviews. Step 5 — Sign the contract: once accepted, sign the written internship contract with the company. Step 6 — Start the apprenticeship: attend vocational school and perform practical activities in the company according to the official training plan.
### Cantonal Support and Resources
The cantonal office for vocational education and training of the canton of Glarus provides free counseling to parents and interested young people. It offers information on available positions, collective agreements, indicative salaries, and funding or contributions for apprentices in financial difficulty. At the federal level, the State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (SERI) provides information on legal rights and duties, as well as access to national internship search platforms.
To assess your economic position and understand how the apprentice salary might impact your personal budget, it is useful to use [salary calculators](nav:calculator) that allow you to simulate net incomes according to cantonal and federal taxes. This tool allows you to plan the internship period and expected income with greater awareness.

item.title: Apprenticeship and training: how it works in Switzerland
item.description: Find out how apprenticeships work in Switzerland: from traineeship research to contract, from pay to legal protections to professional maturity.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Dual apprenticeship: 3-4 years of company practice + vocational school - Federal legal protection: maximum hours, minimum holidays, mandatory social contributions - Nationally recognized Practical Training Certificate (CFC) - Subsequent access to professional maturity and university education
## Key facts - **What**: Dual professional training (practice + theoretical teaching) with CFC certificate - Duration: 3-4 years depending on the sector and type of certificate - Where: Every canton (including Glarus), at registered companies and recognized vocational schools - Who: Apprentices, companies, vocational schools, Cantonal Training Offices - Protection: Wage rights, maximum hours, minimum holidays, mandatory social insurances (AVS/AI/LAINF)
Apprenticeship represents the main professional training path in Switzerland, a dual system that combines practical training in a company with theoretical teaching in a school. In every canton, including Glarus, thousands of companies offer apprenticeship positions in various sectors: from commerce to craftsmanship, from industry to services and healthcare.
Those who undertake an apprenticeship work in a company registered in the cantonal lists, learning a trade under the guidance of a training master. At the same time, they attend general and theoretical training lessons at a recognized vocational school, usually 1-2 days a week. The total duration is usually 3 or 4 years, depending on the sector and the type of certificate pursued.
### Structure and certification
The path allows obtaining a Practical Training Certificate (CFC), recognized at the national level and spendable on the Swiss job market. After the CFC, those who wish can access professional maturity, a title that opens the doors to professional universities (SUP) without an admission exam. There is also the Basic Certificate (CFP), a 2-year path aimed at those with learning difficulties.
Apprenticeship is regulated by federal legislation on professional training, which sets common standards for the whole of Switzerland. However, each canton has competence on local organizational details and supervision of training, through the respective Cantonal Office of Professional Training.
### Legal protection of the worker
As an employee, the apprentice is protected by federal labor law norms. They cannot be exploited: the weekly working hours are limited (maximum 45 hours in industry, offices, and sales; 50 hours in other sectors), the minimum holidays are guaranteed (4 weeks per year, 5 if a minor), and the weekly rest is inviolable. During their stay at the company, the apprentice receives a salary agreed upon in the apprenticeship contract, from which social security contributions are deducted.
Social security contributions (AVS/AI/IPG, LAINF/LAA) are mandatory and paid by the employer or deducted from the salary according to contractual modalities. Health insurance (LAMal/KVG), which in Switzerland is private and mandatory for residents, remains the responsibility of the apprentice (with possible cantonal subsidies for young people with low income).
At the conclusion of the apprenticeship, the CFC is issued, a fundamental document for any subsequent employment in the sector. ### Compensation and salary bands
During the apprenticeship, compensation varies significantly depending on the sector, the cantonal region, and the year of training. There is no federal minimum wage in Switzerland, but many cantons have introduced their own. Additionally, some sectors have collective labor agreements that set minimum wages for apprentices, often with predetermined annual increases.
Generally, the initial salary is lower than that of a qualified worker with the same CFC, but it increases progressively over the years of training. Part of the workday is dedicated to school attendance, during which the apprentice is not physically at the company but still receives compensation. Sometimes the pay slip separately lists practical work days and school days.
### Social contributions and mandatory insurance
The employer automatically pays social security contributions. The apprentice's share for AVS/AI/IPG is 5.3%, while the total (including the employer's contribution) is 10.6%. The work accident insurance (LAINF/LAA) varies by sector (from about 0.7% to 1.5%) and is entirely the company's responsibility.
Health insurance is private: the apprentice must take out insurance within 3 months of the first day of work, choosing a fund from the many available in the canton of residence. There are different deductibles (from CHF 300 to CHF 2500 annually) and coverage models. Each canton offers forms of subsidy for young people with low income. To verify the calculation of your gross-net salary based on social contributions, consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator).
### Apprenticeship contract: rights and obligations
The apprenticeship contract is a mandatory legal document that must contain: - Start date and total duration of the apprenticeship - Monthly (or daily) salary - Weekly work schedule and school attendance days - Number of annual vacation days (minimum 4 weeks, 5 if a minor) - Duration of the probationary period (usually 1-2 months) - Cause and manner of early termination - Identification of the apprenticeship master and the vocational school
Once the probationary period is over, the contract cannot be terminated by either party without just cause (disciplinary reasons, insolvency, significant change in circumstances). If there is a disagreement about termination, the cantonal conciliation office can intervene.
### Minors and additional protections
If the apprentice is a minor, Swiss law provides additional protections: reduced hours compared to adults, absolute prohibition of night work and particularly dangerous tasks, and mandatory supervision by the apprenticeship master. The minimum vacation increases to 5 weeks per year for those under 20 at the time of signing the contract.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to find an internship
The first step is to identify the sector and the profession of interest. In Switzerland, thousands of professions are accessible through apprenticeships, from bricklayers to nurses, from cooks to electricians, from logistics to graphic designers. Each canton has an official catalog of learnable trades.
The main search channels are: - **National online portals**: many cantons manage websites where all available internship ads are published, organized by sector and location. - Cantonal training office: contact the canton's office directly where you wish to follow the internship (e.g., the one in Glarus for local internships). It provides guidance and lists accredited companies. - Local companies: go directly to companies in the sector of interest with a CV and cover letter, even if they do not have published ads. - School guidance: secondary schools offer professional guidance services and report local opportunities. - Trade associations: professional orders, unions, and sectoral associations often publish ads and maintain lists of training companies.
Once you have found an interesting ad, prepare a professional application: a concise cover letter explaining the chosen motivation, an updated CV, and possibly a professional photograph. The candidate highlights transferable skills (seriousness, punctuality, ability to learn, teamwork) rather than technical qualifications (which will be acquired during the internship).
### Selection and signing of the contract
Companies select apprentices through interviews, sometimes preceded by an aptitude test or skills (reasoning, manual skills, etc.). During the interview, motivation towards the profession, interest in the company and sector, and teamwork attitude are evaluated.
If accepted by the selection, the candidate and the company sign the internship contract in triplicate (one for the young person, one for the company, one for the cantonal office). Before the first working day, the apprentice must: take out the mandatory health insurance (at the company's request), enroll in the canton's vocational school, and find out about the days and times of lessons.
### Professional Maturity: continuing studies
After obtaining the CFC, those who wish to continue towards tertiary education can access the professional maturity. This title requires 1-2 additional years of training, followed in parallel or subsequently to the CFC, and allows direct enrollment in professional universities (SUP) without an admission exam.
Professional maturity is offered by most cantonal vocational training schools and covers various orientations: technical, commercial, social services, health, design, tourism. Access depends on school results during the apprenticeship.
To find internship ads in your area, consult the national internship search portal and contact the cantonal vocational training office directly. If you have already started an apprenticeship, you can check your gross-net salary with the [salary calculator](nav:calculator).

item.title: Volkswagen cuts another 50,000 jobs
item.description: The Volkswagen Group has announced a restructuring plan that envisages the cutting of an additional 50,000 jobs by 2030.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Volkswagen to cut 50,000 jobs by 2030 - Total job losses: 100,000 (15% of global workforce) - Restructuring plan approved by management and unions
## Key facts - **What**: Volkswagen to cut 50,000 jobs - When: By 2030 - Where: Production sites in Emden, Zwickau, Hannover (VW) and Neckarsulm (Audi) - Who: Volkswagen Group - Amount: 100,000 jobs in total
Volkswagen has announced a harsh restructuring plan that involves cutting an additional 50,000 jobs by 2030. This brings the total job losses to 100,000, approximately 15% of the global workforce. The plan was approved on Thursday and agreed upon by management and unions.
The most affected production sites will be those in Emden, Zwickau, Hannover for VW, and Neckarsulm for Audi. There is no talk of closing these plants at the moment, but the possibility remains on the table.
### Implications for the Volkswagen Group
In addition to reducing the workforce, the “Future Plan 2030” aims to halve its model range by 2035. According to the economic magazine Wirtschaftswoche, Volkswagen could withdraw the Spanish brand Seat from the market, with its closure expected by 2029 at the latest.
Chairman of the Supervisory Board Hans Dieter Pötsch stated that the implementation of the new plan “will ensure the long-term sustainability and competitiveness of the Volkswagen Group.” ## Practical Analysis
Volkswagen's restructuring plan has significant implications not only for the group's employees but also for the global automotive industry. The reduction in the range of models and the possible closure of the Seat brand could have repercussions on the electric and hybrid vehicle market, sectors in which Volkswagen is heavily investing.
### Impact on Production Sites
The production sites in Emden, Zwickau, Hannover, and Neckarsulm will be the most affected. Although immediate closures are not being discussed, the possibility remains on the table, which could lead to further uncertainty for workers and local communities.
### Future of Brands
The possible closure of the Seat brand by 2029 could have a significant impact on the market for compact and affordable vehicles. Seat is known for its economical and innovative models, and its disappearance could leave a void in this market segment.
### Sustainability and Competitiveness
Chairman of the Supervisory Board Hans Dieter Pötsch emphasized that the new plan will ensure the long-term sustainability and competitiveness of the Volkswagen Group. This implies that the group is seeking to better position itself in the global market, despite current difficulties.
### Comparison with the Previous Situation
Before the announcement of the restructuring plan, Volkswagen had already cut 50,000 jobs. The current plan brings the total to 100,000, representing a significant reduction in the global workforce. This comparison shows the extent of the measures taken by the group to address current economic challenges.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## Action: What to do in Switzerland
For Swiss workers who may be affected by staff cuts, it is important to monitor developments and stay informed about Volkswagen Group decisions. In addition, it is advisable to consult the competent authorities to obtain information on workers' rights and possible support measures.
### Step-by-Step Procedure
1. **Monitor developments**: Follow the official news and updates of the Volkswagen Group. 2. Consult the authorities: Contact the competent authorities for information on workers' rights. 3. Seek support: Evaluate possible support measures offered by local or national authorities.
### Tools and Resources
For more information and support, you can consult the [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator) and [comparatore CHF/EUR](nav:exchange) available on the site.

To learn more about the practical implications and get support, see [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator) and [comparatore CHF/EUR](nav:exchange).

item.title: Dead Swiss Soldiers: Young UDC shocks with war video
item.description: The UDC Youth are promoting a yes to the neutrality initiative with a self-produced war film showing a Switzerland at war.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The Young UDC promotes a yes vote on the neutrality initiative with a self-produced war video. - The film shows a Switzerland at war to raise awareness among young people. - Marianne Binder of the Center criticizes the video as misinformation.
## Key facts - **What**: Self-produced war video by the Young UDC. - When: Promotion for the neutrality initiative. - Where: Switzerland. - Who: Young UDC, Marianne Binder (the Center). - Amount: Not specified.
The Young UDC of Switzerland have launched a campaign in support of the neutrality initiative with a self-produced war film that shows a Switzerland at war. The video, which includes scenes of air attacks and dead soldiers, ends with a call to vote yes to ensure peace. Nils Fiechter, president of the Young UDC, states that the video aims to shake young people and make them reflect on the reality of war.
> "We want young people to understand what it means to live in a country at war," Fiechter declared.
Marianne Binder, a member of the Council of States and vice-president of the Center, has strongly criticized the video, calling it misinformation that benefits Putin. Binder argues that the neutrality initiative does not prevent wars but limits international cooperation, making Switzerland more isolated.

item.title: Glarus C Permit: Requirements, Procedures and Application
item.description: Permanent residence in Canton Glarus: guide to C permit requirements, language skills, integration and application procedure with cantonal authorities.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The C permit allows permanent residence in Switzerland without periodic renewal - Requires 10 years of residence (5 for EU/EFTA citizens) - Application at the foreigners' office of the Canton of Glarus - Requires local integration criteria and language skills
## Key facts - **What**: Permanent residence permit C - Who: Foreign citizens residing in Switzerland - Where: Canton of Glarus - Required residence duration: 10 years standard; 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens - Competent authority: Foreigners' Office of Glarus and State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) - Additional requirements: Integration, local languages, stable economic situation
For those living in the Canton of Glarus and intending to settle permanently, the permanent residence permit C represents the longest-term residence title provided by Swiss law. Unlike the residence permit B, which is renewed every 5 years, the permit C offers lasting legal stability, subject to compliance with specific federal and cantonal conditions.
According to the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM), the permit C is granted to foreign citizens who have resided continuously in Switzerland for a certain period: normally 10 years for non-European citizens, reduced to 5 years for citizens of the European Union and the European Free Trade Association (EU/EFTA). In the Canton of Glarus, as in other Swiss cantons, the procedure for issuing the permit follows a specific administrative path that includes the evaluation of local integration criteria, acquisition of local language skills, and verification of the applicant's economic and tax situation.
The issuance of the permit C is not a mere formality: the cantonal administrations are required to verify that the candidate has effectively integrated into the local community, demonstrates a stable source of income, and does not pose a risk to public safety. In some exceptional cases, it is possible to anticipate the standard residence term, but this depends on specific circumstances evaluated case by case by the competent cantonal office.
### Difference between permit B and permit C
The residence permit B, renewable every 5 years, is granted to foreign citizens temporarily admitted to work and reside in Switzerland. The permit C, on the other hand, eliminates this renewal cycle: once obtained, it does not need to be renewed, unless the holder loses the right due to security reasons or failed integration. This change of status represents a fundamental step in the life of those who choose Switzerland as a stable residence.
The transition from permit B to permit C directly affects many aspects of life in Switzerland, primarily the tax regime. Permanent residents in the Canton of Glarus are subject to ordinary federal, cantonal, and municipal taxation, just like any other resident, without temporary restrictions. Federal direct tax (IFD), cantonal and municipal taxes are calculated on the same scale as long-term residents, without discrimination based on migratory status. Furthermore, permit C determines the mandatory participation in Swiss pension schemes. Those who work are automatically enrolled in the Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance (AVS) and the Disability Insurance (AI), with contributions amounting to 5.3% of gross salary for the employee, totaling 10.6% with the employer's contribution. If the employment contract includes a pension fund (LPP), the coordination itself depends on the duration and age class: the coordination deduction and the amounts of mandatory contributions vary according to federal criteria. Mandatory enrollment in health insurance (LAMal) must occur within 3 months of arrival in Switzerland and remains an obligation even with permit C. Unlike social security systems, LAMal is a private insurance with per capita premiums, with annual deductibles that each canton regulates in part, and with the possibility of reducing premiums according to cantonal income criteria. ### Access to Credit and Real Estate Ownership With permit C, access to bank credit for the purchase or renovation of real estate becomes significantly easier. Swiss banks consider permit C as an indicator of stability and credibility, increasing the willingness to grant mortgages at favorable rates. For the rental of housing, permit C does not eliminate federal tenant protection rules (Code of Obligations art. 253 ff.), but increases the landlord's trust at the time of signing a contract, reducing the likelihood of being rejected for temporary reasons. Permanent residence, finally, facilitates access to public services and cantonal benefits — scholarships, housing subsidies, integration programs — often reserved for stable residents.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). The application for the C residence permit must be submitted to the competent foreigner's office of the Canton of Glarus. Although the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) sets federal guidelines, each canton adopts specific procedures and forms; it is therefore essential to contact the Glarus administration directly to know the exact documentation required and the processing times. In general, the documentation to be collected includes a residence certificate, extracts from the civil register, documentation relating to work activity or source of income (contracts, payslips, tax declaration), local integration certificates, proof of adequate knowledge of the local German language, a declaration of absence of debts towards the cantonal and municipal tax administration, and certificates of good conduct. Processing times vary depending on the administrative workload of the cantonal office and the completeness of the documentation submitted. Generally, a complete file is processed within 2-4 months, but additional weeks may be required during peak periods. If the application is accepted, the C permit is issued, valid for the entire duration of residence in Switzerland, as long as the holder maintains tax residence in the country. In case of refusal, the cantonal authority is required to communicate the reasons; there is the possibility to appeal within set deadlines to a higher administrative authority. To understand the tax implications of permanent residence in the Canton of Glarus, use our [salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate your actual tax burden. If you have questions about mandatory pension insurance (AVS/LPP), consult the [pension guide](nav:pension). For further specific procedural information of the Canton of Glarus, contact the local foreigner's office or the State Secretariat for Migration directly.

item.title: Glarus C Permit: Requirements and How to Apply
item.description: Complete guide to residence permit C in the canton of Glarus: years of residence required, integration, application procedures and transition to naturalization.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit C requires 10 years residence (5 years for EU/EFTA) - It does not expire, unlike permit B - Opens access to naturalization after an additional 10 years - Obliges federal, cantonal and municipal taxation
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit C (long-term permanent residence) - Duration required: 10 years for non-EU; 5 years for EU/EFTA - Validity: No expiry (non-renewable) - Canton: Glarus (north-eastern Switzerland) - Requirements: Continuous residence, integration, economic stability - Next step: Access to naturalization after 10 years of possession
Residence permit C is the permanent residence status in Switzerland. Those who intend to move permanently to the canton of Glarus must meet the requirements of the federal law SEM (Secretariat of State for Migration) and the specific cantonal regulations.
The application for a C permit in the canton of Glarus normally requires 10 years of uninterrupted residence on Swiss territory for citizens not belonging to the European Union or the European Free Trade Association (EFTA). For citizens of EU and EFTA countries, the period is reduced to 5 years. Unlike the B permit, the C permit has no expiration date and does not require periodic renewals: once obtained, it remains valid indefinitely as long as you maintain your residence in the canton.
### How long before getting the C permit
There is no single deadline for submitting the application: ## Practical implications: naturalization, tax and rights
The C permit is the bridge to ordinary naturalization in Switzerland. Once obtained, you can start counting the years towards the application for Swiss citizenship. Federal law prescribes that ordinary naturalization requires the C permit already in possession, plus a further 10 years of uninterrupted residence (during which periods between the 8th and 18th year of residence count as double in the calculation), in addition to the specific requirements of the canton of Glarus and your municipality of residence, such as adequate language skills, a clean criminal record and social integration.
From a tax perspective, the C permit has direct and important consequences. As soon as you obtain the status, you become subject to full taxation in Switzerland at three levels: federal (federal direct tax of the Federal Tax Administration, FTA/ESTV), cantonal (each canton has its own brackets and rates) and municipal (each municipality applies a multiplier on the cantonal tax base). The canton of Glarus, like all other cantons, publishes its tax rates annually; your municipality of residence within the canton adds a specific local multiplier. This means that your annual tax return must include all earnings, investments and properties within Swiss territory.
From a work perspective, the C permit allows you to exercise any dependent or self-employed profession in the canton of Glarus and the rest of Switzerland without restrictions. Unlike the B permit (residence permit), which in some cantons has sectoral limitations, the C permit offers total freedom of professional choice. You can access public jobs, practice free professions and start economic activities independently.
Finally, the C permit subjects you to the mandatory contributions of Swiss social security: as an employee, you pay 5.3% of your salary towards AHV (old-age and survivors' insurance) and IV (disability insurance). If employed, you are also obliged to the LPP (pension fund, second pillar), with contributions that vary by age group. The LPP is managed by the pension fund of your employer and represents your mandatory private pension fund.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to apply in the canton of Glarus: step-by-step procedure
The application for a C permit in the canton of Glarus must be submitted to the Immigration Office (cantonal designation: Amt für Migration or similar; the exact name can be found on the official website of the canton). The procedure follows these fundamental steps:
Step 1: Check personal prerequisites
Before submitting your application, ensure that you have completed the required residence period (10 years for non-EU/EFTA; 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens). Also, verify that your economic situation is stable: the canton of Glarus requires that you have sufficient income to support yourself without relying on social benefits. Prepare a clean criminal record (requestable from your municipality of residence).
Step 2: Gather the required documentation
The canton of Glarus generally requires: valid identity document (passport, national ID card); current employment contract (if employed) or self-employment declaration, residence certificate issued by your municipality, criminal record, civil status certificate (if married, with marriage certificate), integration declaration (the canton evaluates knowledge of the German language and integration into the local community). For citizens with family members, additional documents may be required.
Step 3: Complete the form and submit the application
The Immigration Office provides the official application form (available on the canton of Glarus website or directly at the office). Fill out the form in all required sections and sign it. Submit the application at the office, along with the complete documentation. Some cantons allow submission by certified mail; check the specific procedures with the cantonal office.
Step 4: Follow the procedure and await the decision
The canton of Glarus will acknowledge receipt of your application and provide a file number. Processing times vary, but the canton generally provides a first communication within 4-8 weeks. It may request additional documents or clarifications. The final decision will be notified in writing by the canton. If approved, you will receive the C permit (physical or digital document, depending on the cantonal system).
### After receiving the C permit
Once you have obtained the C permit, you can register it with your municipality of residence. The permit remains valid indefinitely as long as you continue to reside in the canton. It does not need to be renewed periodically. However, if you change your municipality of residence within the canton, or if you move to another Swiss canton, you must notify the change of residence to the competent authorities (the new canton may require confirmation of your situation).
To subsequently access ordinary naturalization, count from this moment the additional 10 years required. When you reach the term, you can submit an application for naturalization with your municipality of residence in the canton of Glarus.

item.title: Cressier stopped, petrol guaranteed by stocks
item.description: Cressier refinery down for technical failure this week. It covers 30% of Swiss needs. Mandatory stocks guarantee the supply of petrol, diesel and kerosene.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Cressier refinery shut down this week due to technical failure - Covers 30% of Switzerland's gasoline, diesel, and kerosene needs - Federal mandatory reserves ensure continuity of supply
## Key facts - **What**: Technical shutdown of the Cressier refinery in the canton of Neuchâtel - When: Current week, likely to continue into the next week - Where: Cressier, canton of Neuchâtel, Switzerland - Who: FOAG (Federal Office for National Economic Supply) - Importance: The plant covers 30% of the national demand for petroleum products - Annual production: Approximately 3 million tons of gasoline, diesel, kerosene, and other derivatives - Guarantee: Mandatory reserves equivalent to about 4.5 months of average demand for gasoline and diesel
According to the Federal Office for National Economic Supply (FOAG), the supply of gasoline, diesel, and other petroleum products remains guaranteed in Switzerland despite the shutdown of the Cressier refinery in the canton of Neuchâtel, caused by a technical failure. The plant had to stop production this week and is likely to remain out of service next week as well. The severity of the situation is highlighted by the fact that the refinery covers just over 30 percent of Switzerland's demand for petroleum products.
### The pillar of Swiss supply
Cressier, since the closure of the Collombey refinery in 2015, is the only oil refinery still in operation in Switzerland. Each year, it produces approximately three million tons of gasoline, diesel, heating oil, aviation fuel, and other petroleum products. The crude oil arrives in Cressier via a pipeline from the Mediterranean port of Fos-sur-Mer, located near Marseille in France. The rest of Switzerland's demand is largely covered by already refined petroleum products imported from abroad through international commercial channels.
### A two-front crisis: failure and Rhine drought
The shutdown comes at a time of already tense energy supply. For several weeks, the low water level of the Rhine has made it difficult to supply petroleum products via waterways, thus complicating river imports. This double criticality—the failure of the country's only refinery and the transport problem caused by the drought—had led the FOAG to issue a press release on Friday to reassure the market and citizens about the continuity of supplies. In case of temporary shortages, the mandatory reserves can be dispensed in a targeted manner to support the market. ### Mandatory stocks: the national security buffer
The Confederation is not unprepared in the face of shortage scenarios. The mandatory stocks of gasoline and diesel, accumulated in peacetime according to federal economic protection directives, basically correspond to the average requirement of about four and a half months for each product. Should temporary shortfalls loom, targeted withdrawal from these strategic reserves could effectively support the market and fill any gaps in supply. In other words, the inhabitants of Switzerland have a safety belt designed exactly for critical situations such as this: a stationary refinery, a compromised main transport route, and the need for energy continuity.
### The Lesson of 2015: When the System Worked
A similar precedent had already occurred in 2015, eleven years ago. On thatoccasion, Cressier's refinery was shut down for several weeks due to a technical failure. At the same time, the low level of the Rhine made it difficult to import petroleum products by river, creating an even more critical situation than at present. The Confederation then decided to release the compulsory stocks, thus guaranteeing the continuity of supply without interruptions in the civil and industrial sectors, from households to public transport, up to manufacturing companies and hospital services.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### How the mandatory stock mechanism works
Mandatory stocks of petroleum products are not a virtual resource: they are physically stored in refineries, port terminals, and specialized depots strategically distributed across the Swiss national territory. Each fuel supplier and distributor is legally obliged to maintain sufficient reserves to ensure supply continuity in case of crisis. When an emergency occurs—such as a failure of a critical plant, disruption of transport lines, geopolitical crisis, or drought that blocks rivers—the AEP authorizes the coordinated withdrawal from these strategic reserves. The process is rapid: federal authorities, in direct contact with storage facility managers, order the gradual release of stocks to maintain the balance between supply and demand in the national market.
### What changes for Swiss citizens and businesses
For the average citizen and small and medium-sized Swiss businesses, the shutdown of Cressier does not entail any immediate change in daily life. Fuel pumps will continue to operate normally in the coming days, gasoline and diesel prices will not experience sudden and sharp fluctuations (unless further unforeseen external complications arise), and car tanks can be filled without quantity restrictions. The situation is therefore under control by the federal authorities. The only theoretical warning: if the situation were to degenerate into a prolonged crisis—a scenario that federal authorities intend to avoid precisely thanks to the existence of mandatory stocks—then Sunday driving bans or fuel rationing could become relevant, extreme measures but provided for in the federal legislation on the economic supply of the country.
### Staying informed and consulting official updates
The AEP has stated that it is monitoring the situation in real-time, and updates on the duration of the refinery shutdown and the possible need to resort to mandatory stocks should arrive in the coming days through official press releases. Meanwhile, the Confederation maintains the highest level of alert and coordinates with international partners to ensure that no bottlenecks are created in the supply lines. Anyone wishing to stay informed about the developments of the national energy supply and the factors influencing the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) can consult the official updates of the AEP and monitor the data of the energy sector. To better understand how these dynamics impact your real purchasing power, you can use the [salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator) to evaluate your personal budget.

item.title: Buying a house in Nidvaldo: prices, mortgage and taxation
item.description: Buying a house in Switzerland requires you to navigate between three levels of taxation, mortgage and notary fees. Learn how the system works and how to assess loan sustainability.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Three levels of taxation: federal, cantonal, municipal on every real estate purchase - Minimum own funds 20% according to standard Swiss banking practice - Transfer tax varies by canton; notary fees to be agreed with the notary
## Key facts - **What**: Real estate purchase in Switzerland subject to multi-level taxation - Levels: Federal (IFD) + Cantonal + Municipal (local multiplier) - Transfer tax: Specific for canton; rate and taxable person vary - Own funds: Minimum 20% of the real estate value (banking criterion) - Mortgage loan: Max 80% of the value; accrual depends on disposable income
Buying a home in the Canton of Nidvaldo, as in the whole of Switzerland, means interfacing with a tax system divided into three levels: federal, cantonal and municipal. Each tier applies its own rates and regulations. In the specific case of the sale of real estate, the Nidvaldo Canton — like all Swiss cantons — has its own regulations regarding transfer tax, a tax that affects the transfer of ownership. This tax varies significantly between the cantons: the rate, the taxable person (seller or buyer), and the methods of payment follow the cantonal laws. At the same time, notary fees are due (notary fees, registration in the land register, certificates), which must be agreed directly with the notary.
The mortgage loan remains the instrument of The Swiss mortgage: how it works and the bank criteria
In Switzerland, the standard banking practice requires having at least 20% of the property value as own funds (equity). The remaining 80% can be covered by a mortgage, subject to bank approval based on creditworthiness and repayment capacity. This scheme is well-established in the Swiss financial market and serves as the starting point for negotiations with banks.
Own funds can come from personal savings, private pension (third pillar, 3a), or early withdrawal from professional pension (LPP / Pension Fund). LPP is mandatory for all employees in Switzerland and covers the coordinated salary (the difference between gross salary and a coordination threshold set by law). LPP contribution rates vary by age class: 7% for ages 25 to 34, 10% for ages 35 to 44, 15% for ages 45 to 54, and 18% from age 55 until the reference age. These contributions are automatically deducted from the monthly paycheck.
The sustainability of the mortgage is the decisive criterion for loan approval. Banks analyze the ratio between the monthly installment (capital plus interest) and the net available income of the buyer. There is no federal minimum wage in Switzerland (although some cantons have adopted their own), so the assessment of repayment capacity depends on individual income, monthly expenses, and overall financial situation.
Those buying a home must also consider other recurring costs: premiums for mandatory health insurance (LAMal), which vary by canton and risk class and must be taken out within 3 months of purchase or arrival in the country, property insurance (liability and damage), municipal tax (variable by canton and municipality), and possible renovation work. To better understand how to manage pension planning in view of the purchase, consult our [pension comparator](nav:pension).
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step purchase procedure: what to do and which documents are needed
The purchase of a house in Switzerland follows a well-defined formal procedure, marked by precise deadlines and legal obligations.
**Step 1: Financial capacity assessment.** Before even looking for a property, it is essential to contact a bank and verify how much money can be borrowed given your income situation. Banks require income documentation: pay slips for the last 12 months, employment certificate, tax return, extract from the protest register.
Step 2: Search and offer. Once the property has been identified, a written offer is made including the price, terms of sale, and deadlines (property inspection, finalization of financing).
Step 3: Mortgage application. The bank evaluates the creditworthiness of the buyer and the sustainability of the mortgage in relation to income and assets. This process usually takes 2-4 weeks.
Step 4: Notarial deed and registration. Once the mortgage is approved, the parties appear before the notary for the signing of the deed of sale. The notary draws up the deed, collects the signatures, and ensures the registration of the property in the cantonal land register.
Step 5: Payment and delivery. The money (mortgage + own funds) is transferred and the property is delivered to the buyer. The buyer becomes the official owner from the moment of registration in the land register.
Step 6: LAMal subscription (if necessary). If the buyer is not already insured with a Swiss health insurance fund, they must take out compulsory health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months of the purchase (or arrival in the country if foreign). LAMal is a private insurance policy with per capita premiums that vary by canton, age class, and risk class.
Documents needed for the purchase: passport or identity document, pay slip and employment certificate, tax return for the last year, extract from the protest register, bank pre-approval letter, if married: spouse's identity document and declaration of common assets.
During the process, it is prudent to be assisted by an independent mortgage advisor or a tax specialist, especially to understand local tax implications (transfer tax, possible VAT on renovations), the long-term sustainability of the mortgage, and tax saving opportunities.

item.description: The German restructuring of the colossus will hit Feintool and few others. Analysis of the impact on the Swiss industrial square according to Zurich analysts.

## In brief - Volkswagen cuts 50'000 jobs and reduces production from 12 to 9 million vehicles - Feintool (Berne) at risk: stock down 3% in Zurich this morning - Limited impact on other suppliers (Autoneum, SFS, EMS-Chemie, Komax)
## Key facts - **What**: Radical restructuring of the Volkswagen Group with model range reduction - Where: German plants; repercussions on Swiss automotive industry suppliers - Who: Volkswagen AG; analysts from Kepler-Cheuvreux, Vontobel, Zurich Cantonal Bank - Layoffs: 50,000 jobs worldwide - Production: Reduced from 12 to 9 million vehicles per year - Simplification: 75% of the model range by 2035
The colossal restructuring of the Volkswagen Group will shake the Swiss industrial scene? Not entirely. According to analysts, the economic impact for Swiss suppliers will mostly be contained. But one Bernese company risks coming under pressure: Feintool, specialized in precision components, saw its stock price drop by over 3% on the news of the German restructuring.
Volkswagen has announced an unprecedented operation. Fifty thousand jobs eliminated worldwide. Production capacity will be adjusted from twelve million vehicles per year (pre-pandemic) to around nine. Four German plants will lose continuity guarantees beyond 2031–2034. The model range will decrease by 50% by 2035, with a simplification of the offer equal to 75%.
### Feintool in the spotlight
Torsten Sauter, analyst at the multinational financial services company Kepler-Cheuvreux, explains Feintool's vulnerability in concrete terms: "It is the most exposed company because it depends relatively directly on the production volumes and utilization rate of the European automotive industry." The market knows it. This morning on the Zurich stock exchange, the stock fell by over 3%, the most visible sign of investor concern about the dynamics of the Bernese supplier.
But the rest of the landscape is not in turmoil. Autoneum, a specialist in acoustic insulation, has a dependence on Volkswagen estimated at between 5 and 7%, according to Arben Hasanaj of Vontobel. For SFS (fastening components), EMS-Chemie (various materials), and Komax (wiring machines), the risk of significant repercussions remains marginal. Even the closure of German plants does not automatically mean a global volume contraction: Volkswagen intends to concentrate production, better saturating the remaining plants. "Produced volumes are more decisive than the number of plants or employees," according to Walter Bamert, analyst at the Zurich Cantonal Bank (ZKB), who defines the situation as a "storm in a teacup." ### Swiss industry already in reorientation
Swiss suppliers do not see this crisis as a sudden shock. In recent years the European automotive sector has suffered from chronic pressure: high costs, weak demand, growing competition from China. Swiss companies have already adapted. According to Vontobel, Swiss suppliers have restructured their operations and diversified their customer base, shifting an increasing share of turnover to Asian markets, particularly China.
This strategic transition could paradoxically prove to be an advantage. If Volkswagen accelerates automation to reduce costs, companies like Komax (which specializes in wiring machines) could even benefit. Increasing industrial productivity requires sophisticated tools, not just components. At the same time, those like Autoneum who remain anchored to European volumes will face margin pressures, but their limited exposure (5–7% from Volkswagen businesses) limits potential damage.
### The Differential Between Direct and Indirect Dependence
The real lesson of the Volkswagen rearrangement is that vulnerability depends on the degree of dependence on volumes. Feintool is exposed because it produces components that the automotive customer cannot do without, in quantities proportional to production. If VW cuts 25% of the vehicles, Feintool cuts 25% of the turnover related to that customer.

The Foreign Policy Committee of the Council of States (CPE-S) has officially stated its position on the Third Bilateral Agreements between Switzerland and the European Union. After a lengthy analysis process lasting several months, during which the technical and political details of the package of agreements were examined, the majority of the committee expressed a positive recommendation, inviting the upper house to vote in favor of integrating and stabilizing relations between our country and Brussels. ### Towards the autumn session The debate will now move to the Council of States chamber, where the issue will be addressed during the next autumn parliamentary session, scheduled for the end of the month. This step represents a crucial moment for the national political agenda, as the final decision on the line to be adopted will influence future cooperation dynamics with Switzerland's main trading partner. Members of the Council of States will be called upon to carefully weigh the benefits of diplomatic and economic stability against concerns related to national sovereignty and the management of migration flows. At the same time, wage protection remains a topic of extreme relevance, especially with regard to maintaining worker protection standards in Swiss territory. Another central element, strongly requested by various political parties, is the inclusion of a specific safeguard clause. This measure aims to intervene in cases of excessive immigration, allowing for more controlled management of flows in situations of particular pressure on the labor market or national infrastructure. The discussion will not be limited exclusively to the content of the treaties but will also touch on the legal form that these must assume.

## In brief - Heatwaves and drought hit Swiss agriculture - Estimated losses of 522 million francs in 2026 - Price increases for milk and potatoes
## Key facts - **What**: Agricultural losses due to heatwave and drought - When: 2026 - Where: Switzerland - Who: Swiss Farmers' Union (SFU) - Amount: 522 million francs
Zurich - The heatwaves and prolonged drought that hit Switzerland this summer are leaving a deep mark on the agricultural sector. With decimated harvests and soaring production costs for forced irrigation, the economic consequences are now directly affecting prices, with increases already decided for milk and potatoes.
According to estimates by the Swiss Farmers' Union (SFU), the total losses for Swiss agriculture will amount to 522 million francs in 2026. "This figure matches the losses of 2003, another year characterized by a record heatwave," a spokesperson told the Awp agency.
### Agricultural Losses The picture painted by the SFU is dramatic: it is estimated that 50% of the grain maize harvest has been lost, while losses for forage maize reach 30%. Potatoes and sugar beets both show a 20% drop, while soybeans, sunflowers, and fresh vegetables see a 10% reduction. Fresh fruits experience a 5% contraction, but it is mainly forage activities, such as hay, that are hit hard, with losses reaching 40%. ### Impact on Prices The most alarming figure concerns potatoes. According to the Swisspatat industry organization, the 2026 production stopped at 333,000 tonnes, the lowest level ever recorded. Compared to the 2020-2025 five-year average (411,000 tonnes), there is a drop of almost 20%. To meet demand, Switzerland will have to import around 130,000 tonnes of tubers. The prospects for sugar beets are also bleak, with an estimated loss of 25,000 tonnes, according to preliminary calculations by the Swiss Beet Growers Federation. The fruit sector has not been spared. The Fruit-Union Suisse industry association reports a cherry harvest 15% lower than expected and similar problems for plums and raspberries, whose plants have suffered particularly from the heat and drought. "For the vegetables that are growing now and will be harvested in autumn for storage, smaller sizes and lower quantities should be expected," anticipates Markus Waber, deputy director of the Swiss Vegetable Producers Union (USPV). ### Price Increases In the face of these losses and the higher costs incurred for irrigation, agricultural organizations have initiated negotiations to adjust prices. For milk, an indicative increase of four cents per liter has already been decided, and the sector will ask the Confederation for additional support of four cents to cope with the emergency. In the potato sector, producers have secured a price increase of just two cents per kilogram from the large distribution chains. A figure deemed insufficient by Martin Rufer, director of the USC: "It is clearly insufficient to mitigate the economic consequences of the drought. We had asked for an increase of seven cents for conventional potatoes and thirteen cents for organic ones."

## Key facts - **What**: Accelerating the Swiss economy - When: Second quarter 2026 - Where: Switzerland - Who: Dry - Amount: 1.5% GDP growth
The Swiss economy is showing stronger-than-expected signs of growth. According to data published on 3 September 2026 by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), Swiss Gross Domestic Product, adjusted for the effects of sporting events, increased by 1.5% compared to the previous quarter, after the +0.5% recorded in the first three months of the year. This is the highest quarterly growth rate since the third quarter of 2021.
### Industry and Growth Sectors
But what is behind this acceleration? And, above all, how much can it translate into more opportunities for those who work in Switzerland or are thinking of becoming border workers? The most obvious data comes from the industry. In the second quarter, value creation in the industrial sector increased by 3.9%, while the manufacturing sector made even more substantial progress, at 4.5%. The result was mainly driven by the chemical and pharmaceutical industry, which grew by 10.5% after some decidedly less brilliant quarters. Exports also made an important contribution to the recovery.
The report ## Implications for Frontiersmen
Switzerland's economic growth has significant implications for frontier workers, who represent an important part of the country's workforce. The recovery in the industrial and manufacturing sector could translate into new job opportunities and an increase in the demand for skilled labour. This could be particularly beneficial for Italian workers who cross the border every day to work in Switzerland.
### Labour Market
The labour market is also sending positive signals. Widespread growth in various sectors could lead to greater employment stability and new career opportunities for frontier workers. However, it is important to note that SECO has warned that the growth of the chemical-pharmaceutical sector may not be sustainable in the long term, which could affect the future prospects for workers in this sector.
### Growing Industries
Sectors that showed significant growth include the chemical and pharmaceutical industry, which saw an increase of 10.5%, and manufacturing, which grew by 4.5%. These sectors are traditionally important for the Swiss economy and could offer new job opportunities for frontier workers.
### Services and Transportation
The services sector also saw growth of 0.7%, with financial services and transport showing progress of 1.9%.

For cross-border workers who wish to take advantage of the opportunities offered by Swiss economic growth, it is important to be well-informed and prepared. Here are some concrete steps that can be useful:
### Inform Yourself About Job Opportunities
Cross-border workers should closely monitor job opportunities in growing sectors such as the chemical and pharmaceutical industry, the manufacturing sector, financial services, and transportation. It is useful to consult the websites of Swiss companies and participate in job fairs and networking events.
### Update Your Skills
Economic growth may require new skills and qualifications. Cross-border workers should consider the possibility of participating in training and professional development courses to remain competitive in the Swiss job market.
### Plan for Mobility
Economic growth may lead to increased mobility in the job market. Cross-border workers should be ready to consider new job opportunities in different regions of Switzerland, taking into account local living conditions and infrastructure.
### Use Available Tools
To get a comprehensive overview of job opportunities and economic conditions in Switzerland, cross-border workers can use tools such as the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF/EUR comparator](nav:exchange). These tools can help evaluate job opportunities and plan your career more informedly.
### Conclusion
In conclusion, Swiss economic growth offers new opportunities for cross-border workers. Being well-informed, up-to-date, and ready to seize these opportunities can make a difference for those who wish to work and live in Switzerland. By using available tools and monitoring job market trends, cross-border workers can maximize their prospects for success.
